keyVerseText: These are the generations of the heavens and of the earth when they were created, in the day that the LORD God made the earth and the heavens,
rootMeaning: The Hebrew word תּוֹלְדָה (tôwlᵉdâh) derives from the root יָלַד (yâlad), which means to bear or beget. This root emphasizes the act of giving birth or bringing forth offspring, highlighting the literal sense of generation and descent. Thus, tôwlᵉdâh carries the idea not only of birth but also of the resulting lineage or history that flows from that act of begetting, enriching the common English gloss of "generations" with a dynamic sense of ongoing life and continuity.
usageInScripture: Throughout Scripture, occurring 39 times, תּוֹלְדָה is predominantly used to denote genealogical records or accounts of descendants, as reflected in frequent translations like "by their generations" and "Now these are the generations." Its use consistently points to the unfolding of family lines and historical sequences, whether referring to individuals, clans, or even cosmic history. This range of usage reveals its function as a bridge linking personal lineage with broader historical and theological narratives.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding תּוֹלְדָה enriches our grasp of biblical revelation by emphasizing God's sovereign orchestration of history through generations. It reminds believers that God's covenantal promises are fulfilled not merely in isolated moments but through successive lineages and unfolding history. The term also points to the faithfulness of God in preserving His people across time, underscoring the continuity of His redemptive plan culminating in Christ, the ultimate descendant. Recognizing the weight of generations invites Christians to see their lives as part of a divine genealogy shaped by grace and purpose.
keyVerseReflection: Genesis 2:4 states, "These are the generations of the heavens and of the earth when they were created," using תּוֹלְדָה to introduce the account of creation. Here, the word conveys more than a mere list; it frames the cosmos itself as having a history and origin, underscoring God's creative act as the birth of all things. This usage elevates the concept of "generations" to a cosmic scale, inviting reflection on God as the ultimate source and sustainer of all existence.
